facts.value: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025/26 to Audit and Governance Committee, Tuesday 21 July 2026. Report of Director of Finance and Section 151 Officer; introduced by Head of Finance and Deputy S151 Officer. 20 pages including a five-appendix set (A: investments at 31 March 2026; B: investment counterparties 2025/26; C: MUFG Corporate Markets economic update; D: MUFG interest rate forecasts; E: glossary). Standalone report — Tables 1-9 all in-body, no separate loan-book appendix required because the Council carries no PWLB or market debt. Report Author block on page 9 lists Senior Financial Accountant, Head of Finance, Director of Finance and S151 Officer in order, with emails hanne.birchall@southribble.gov.uk, oliver.dent@southribble.gov.uk, neil.halton@southribble.gov.uk in the same order, telephone 01257 515028 (Chorley area code; South Ribble runs a shared finance service with Chorley). Read in full from local PDF on 2026-08-16.

source.title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025/26 — Audit and Governance Committee, 21 July 2026

facts.note: The role→name mapping is inferred from co-order of the author role list and the email list. The paper does not label individuals against specific titles inside the body. Safe to address Neil Halton as Director of Finance and Section 151 Officer on that basis, but flag the inference on the contact record.

facts.value: TIES ZERO ON ZERO. price_book.py --find "South Ribble" returns 'no borrower matching South Ribble'; --find "Ribble" returns 'no borrower matching Ribble'; and the explicit --as-at 2026-03-31 check on 'SOUTH RIBBLE BOROUGH COUNCIL' returns 'NO LOANS'. Query mechanism verified working — --find "Chorley" returns CHORLEY BOROUGH COUNCIL. Paper Table 4 (page 5): Debt at 1 April £0, Change in Debt £0, Debt at 31 March £0. Only external item at year end is £42k of Other Long Term Liabilities (finance lease residual on the 138 opening less 96 movement). Zero external debt on our file, zero external debt on their table — the two agree exactly. Prudential-limit context: Authorised Limit £36.691m, Operational Boundary £33.355m — both precautionary and neither approached (Council remained well below throughout).

source.title: OUR file — price_book.py --find and --as-at; paper Table 4 (page 5) and paras 21-23 (page 5)

facts.note: Same shape as Rushcliffe (E07000176) and Rochford (E07000075) — the strongest form the loan-book cross-check can take for a debt-free council. Safe to open the email with.
Debt-free council with a growing internally-funded CFR. Balance-sheet identity closes to within a £30k rounding gap in the paper's own numbers.

facts.value: CFR movement TIES to the pound: opening £19,724k + net financing need £6,022k - MRP £620k = closing £25,126k (Table 3, page 4). That is a +£5,402k lift in one year — the CFR grew by 27.4% while external borrowing was zero throughout. The full uplift is being funded from cash balances. Paragraph 31 (page 7) frames this explicitly: 'Given borrowing rates and investment rates are broadly similar, the Council has continued to achieve budget savings by maintaining a position of under borrowing, which means that it has used its own cash balances to finance capital expenditure rather than taking additional external loans.' Net financing need for the year was itself £3,711k under the original estimate (£8,369k) — capital expenditure delivered £15,363k against a £35,038k estimate (Table 1), a £4,864k underspend that reduced the borrowing draw commensurately.
facts.note: This is the strongest hook in the paper for us. A district that grew CFR £5.4m in one year and carries the whole £25.1m internally — priced against the MUFG forecast at Appendix D (10yr PWLB 5.50%, 25yr 6.00% on Jun-26 view, both easing only gradually), there is real money in the position. The observation to make is not that they should borrow — that would be advice — but that as the cash cushion shrinks (average daily balance -£7.4m year-on-year, interest earned -32.97%) the marginal cost of the internal call rises.

facts.value: Total investments £22.342m at 31 March 2026 (Appendix A, page 10; matches Table 6 investments row £22,342k). Composition: £11m of LA term deposits (Bournemouth CCP £5m at 4.50% to 17-Apr-26 placed 7-Nov-25; Blackpool £6m at 4.50% to 30-Jun-26 placed 31-Dec-25); £5.342m in call accounts (Barclays BPA £1.342m at 1.25%; Lloyds BOS £4m at 3.51%); £6m in three money market funds at 3.76-3.82% (Aberdeen Standard, Federated, Blackrock, £2m each). No sums invested over one year (para 29 confirms the £6m maximum-over-365-days limit was not used). Both LA term deposits had matured before the Committee meeting on 21 July 2026. Investment return TIES: Table 9 rows sum to £37,103k average daily balance and £1,503k earnings across all five investment types. Weighted average yield = £1,503k / £37,103k = 4.051%. The paper's headline 3.63% is a simple mean of the five row rates ((3.89+4.35+3.82+2.00+4.09)/5), which the paper itself acknowledges openly at paragraph 34.

source.title: Appendix A (page 10), Table 9 (page 7), Table 6 (page 6), paras 29 and 34

facts.note: Two useful hooks. First, the 3.63% vs 4.05% simple-mean-vs-weighted distinction — paper is transparent about it (para 34), so noting the weighted view is not correcting them, it's engaging with their own disclosure. Second, two LA term deposits at 4.50% for 5-6 month tenors are square-market rates for placements made in Nov/Dec 2025 with Bank Rate stepping down through the year — right in the middle of the LA-to-LA cash market we see from the borrower side.

facts.value: Cash cushion has shrunk materially in 2025/26. Paragraph 35 (page 8): 'The average daily balance of £37.103m shown above is 16.62% less than the 2024/25 figure of £44.498m. Interest earned decreased by 32.97% compared to 2024/25, due to the reduced available cash balances to invest.' Change: -£7.395m in average daily invested balances year-on-year. DMO usage rose by contrast: paragraph 36 states average daily investment with DMO was £4.199m in 2025/26 vs £1.560m in 2024/25 — a +£2.639m shift toward the most liquid instrument as balances fell. Table 6 (page 6) also shows Core Funds / Working Balances actual (£47,456k) against estimate (£58,979k), £11.5m below the strategic estimate.
facts.note: This is the counterweight to the internal-borrowing savings narrative. As core cash falls, the amount of CFR that can be internally financed shrinks; at some point the position has to be re-visited. Not our call to make in the email; simply named as context so the reader can situate para 31's savings claim inside the year-on-year cash trajectory.

Not a distinctive figure at ~3% — different shape from Rushcliffe's -1.33% negative (Rushcliffe has £72.6m of investments against £8.4m CFR; South Ribble has £22.3m against £25.1m CFR). South Ribble is not a net investor in the same sense.

facts.value: MRP Policy: para 17 confirms the 2025/26 MRP Policy was approved as part of the Treasury Strategy on 5 March 2025 and remained unchanged during the year. Total MRP/VRP charge for 2025/26: £620k actual (Table 3, page 4) vs £699k estimate and £517k revised. Prudential indicators (paragraphs 21-23, page 5): Authorised Limit £36.691m — not exceeded (para 22 confirms); Operational Boundary £33.355m — Council remained within throughout (para 23). Paragraph 8: 'The prudential and treasury indicators for 2025/26, approved as part of the Treasury Strategy for 2025/26 to 2027/28 remained unchanged throughout the year and all comparisons made in this report are based on those same indicators.'
facts.note: No policy change to raise, no breach to raise. Standard-shape district outturn.

facts.value: Treasury advisors: Mitsubishi Financial Group (MUFG) Corporate Markets, formerly Link Asset Services (para 32, page 7). MUFG's own economic update (Appendix C, pages 12-14) and interest rate forecast (Appendix D, page 15) attached. Latest MUFG forecast (dated 25.03.26): Bank Rate held at 3.75% through 2026, cutting to 3.50% in Sep-27 then 3.25% by Mar-28 and held there through Mar-29. PWLB rates: 5yr 5.00% (Jun-26) easing to 4.10% (Sep-28 onwards); 10yr 5.50% (Jun-26) easing to 4.60% (Sep-28); 25yr 6.00% (Jun-26) easing to 5.10-5.20%; 50yr 5.80% (Jun-26) easing to 4.90% (Dec-28). MUFG's narrative in Appendix C is measured — energy shock, weak labour market, activity soft; expects rates held at 3.75% this year with cuts leaving Bank rate at 3.5% by end-2027.
facts.note: MUFG's forecast is what the Council is pricing against. Useful as the market anchor for the internal-borrowing observation — long-dated PWLB at 5-6% for the next 12 months on their advisor's own view, easing only gradually. Note: the Link Group forecast printed above it (dated 11.11.24) is the one that was used when the Treasury Strategy was set — outdated by the time of this outturn.

signals.headline: Debt-free district; CFR £25.126m grew £5.402m in the year with zero external borrowing (all internal); investments £22.342m earning weighted 4.05% (paper quotes simple-mean 3.63%, transparent about it); avg daily invested balance down £7.4m vs 2024/25 with interest earned down 32.97% — verified quiet, but the internal-borrowing bet is getting more exposed as cash shrinks
signals.why_it_matters: Nothing alarms. Loan-book reconciliation ties zero on zero. CFR movement (19,724 + 6,022 - 620 = 25,126) ties to the pound. Balance-sheet identity closes to within a £30k rounding gap in the paper's own Under-borrowing arithmetic. Both prudential limits held. MRP policy unchanged. The story is the shape: a growing internally-funded CFR set against a shrinking cash cushion, priced against MUFG's own 25yr PWLB forecast of 6.00% (Jun-26 view) easing only gradually — real money in the position but the room to keep making that bet is narrowing. Two term deposits at 4.50% for 5-6 month tenors are square-market rates for the LA-to-LA window; both had matured before Committee. Paper is transparent about the simple-mean yield calculation (para 34), which lets us engage with the weighted 4.05% view without appearing to correct them.

courses_named: Reading the quarterly & outturn reports (for members)
officer.body:
Hi Neil,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Treasury Management Outturn 2025/26 you took to Audit and Governance on 21 July, ahead of the mid-year review your paragraph 7 flags for the same pattern later this year. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your paper's arithmetic ties all the way through and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

Two cross-checks first, which is where we start on any paper. Our PWLB file returns no entries for South Ribble, and your Table 4 agrees exactly — no debt at 1 April 2025, no change in the year, and £42k of finance-lease residual at 31 March. Zero on zero is the strongest form that check can take. Your Table 3 CFR movement also ties to the pound: opening £19.724m plus the £6.022m net financing need less the £620k MRP equals your £25.126m closing.

What first caught our eye is what sits behind that £25.126m. Your CFR grew by £5.402m in one year — a 27% single-year lift — and every pound of it is being funded from cash. Your paragraph 31 puts the reasoning plainly: because borrowing and investment rates are broadly similar, under-borrowing is a deliberate saving. Against the MUFG forecast you attach at Appendix D, that saving is quite readable — 10-year PWLB at 5.50% on the June 2026 view, 25-year at 6.00%, easing only gradually through the strategy period. Your investment book earned a weighted 4.05% in 2025/26. So on the £5.4m increment the gap between the marginal internal cost you gave up and the long-dated PWLB you did not draw is a real number, and something a member might reasonably ask about. It's also a bet that gets more exposed as core cash falls — paragraph 35 flags interest earned fell nearly a third year-on-year and the average daily balance dropped £7.4m against 2024/25. We don't model your cashflow so nothing follows from us as advice; the /pwlb-activity page just carries the numbers so a member can see the shape of the trade-off between the internal position and the day's long-dated fixings.

On the yield: your Table 9's headline 3.63% is the simple mean of the five row rates — you note this openly in paragraph 34 and it is the honest way to compare across investment types when balances shift during the year. The arithmetic weighted by amount (£1,503k of earnings on £37,103k of average daily balance) works out to about 4.05%, and against the 3.75% Bank Rate you cite that is a fair result on the year. Both are useful for different questions; the weighted view is the one that reads directly against sector yields on our /loan-analysis page.

The two term deposits on your Appendix A both landed at exactly 4.50% for the five-to-six-month tenor — Bournemouth £5m maturing 17 April, Blackpool £6m maturing 30 June, both since paid off. Placed in November and December 2025, those are square-market rates for the tenor in that window. We read the LA-to-LA market from the borrower side across every strategy paper we see, so the platform carries a live view of where that market clears each week — useful when the next term placement is being sized.

One standing observation. The liability benchmark work at our /loan-analysis page is interactive and live, which matters given CIPFA has updates to the Prudential and Treasury Codes coming. Your paper doesn't print a benchmark — few outturn reports do — but running one against the Table 3 CFR trajectory and the Appendix B counterparty ladder would give members a single-page view of when the under-borrowing position starts to bite. Happy to walk through it if useful.

On training, four fit the shape of what you're doing. Reading the quarterly & outturn reports (for members) is a members' course written for exactly the Committee this outturn goes to; Liability benchmark modelling for treasury goes to the observation above; Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets speaks to your Table 7 and Appendix A; and LA Credit Analysis speaks to your Appendix B counterparty framework. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find any of this useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free -> https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn -> https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025/26 — Audit and Governance Committee, 21 July 2026 — http://southribble.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s57901/treasury-management-outturn-report-2025-26-committee-report.pdf
